summary: This informational memo explains the terms and concepts used for benchmarking OSPF. It also discusses how the terms relate to the testing tasks involved, so that tests are described consistently.

plainLanguage.summary: Before you can measure how fast something is, everyone must agree on what the words mean. This is the dictionary for timing OSPF routers.

subtitle: Terminology and concepts for consistent OSPF performance testing.

tldr.problem: OSPF benchmarking requires precise terminology, but key terms are defined differently across documents and implementations, leading to confusion about what is being measured.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC collects definitions of measurement approaches (white box vs black box), link types, timers, and the core concept of single-router convergence, relating each to OSPF benchmarking specifically.
tldr.outcome: Engineers and vendors can now use consistent terminology to describe OSPF performance tests and results.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This RFC is a companion document to RFC 4061, which defines OSPF benchmarking tests. While RFC 4061 describes how to run tests, this document explains what the tests measure and what the terms mean. Consistent terminology is essential for comparing measurements across vendors and implementations.

The document covers three kinds of definitions: well-known industry terms that apply to benchmarking in general, OSPF-specific terms defined elsewhere (like in RFC 2328, the OSPF standard), and new concepts introduced by OSPF benchmarking work, particularly the idea of single-router convergence.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of this as the footnotes section for the benchmarking rulebook. It explains what each word means so everyone is on the same page.

sections.title: Measurement Approaches
sections.content:
White box (or internal) measurements are taken on the router being tested, using internal timers and debug output. White box measurements reveal what the router is actually doing but can be hard to compare across vendors, since different implementations report times differently and some provide more detailed output than others. White box tests can also affect the results by adding processing load.

Black box (or external) measurements infer router behavior by watching what it transmits to other devices. For example, when a downstream device receives all the routing information, you can infer that the upstream router has finished flooding. Black box measurements are comparable across vendors but include propagation delays and other factors beyond the router's processing. For OSPF benchmarking, external (black box) techniques are more practical.
sections.plainLanguage: White box is like a timer on the runner's chest; you see exactly what the router does but it is messy to compare. Black box is like a stopwatch watching the finish line; it is fair across runners but includes the travel time to the line.

sections.title: Link Types and Timers
sections.content:
Point-to-point links are simple direct connections between two routers. They converge faster than broadcast links because there is no need for designated router (DR) election overhead. Broadcast links connect more than two routers on a shared medium (like Ethernet). All routers on a broadcast link must form adjacencies with the DR and BDR (backup DR), and flooding is asynchronous, happening through the DR—this adds latency.

Two critical timers control OSPF behavior on each link type. The Hello Interval is how often a router sends hello messages; all routers on the same link must use the same value. The Router Dead Interval is the timeout: if a router does not receive hellos from a neighbor within this time, the neighbor is considered down. Decreasing these timers speeds up failure detection and convergence but increases protocol overhead.
sections.plainLanguage: Point-to-point is a phone call between two people; broadcast is a meeting. Hellos are check-in messages, and the dead interval is how long you wait before assuming someone has left.

sections.title: Single Router Convergence
sections.content:
In networking, convergence usually means the entire network reaching a stable state with loop-free paths. For benchmarking, convergence is redefined to mean a single router reacting to a topology change. From the router's perspective, convergence is complete when it has flooded any new information it received, recalculated its shortest path tree, and updated its routing table with new paths.

This narrower definition is practical for testing because it isolates a single device's performance. Importantly, convergence time does not include the time for the data plane (forwarding engine) to receive the new routes or begin forwarding packets—only the control plane work. This distinction is crucial: a router might finish its control plane update quickly, but the hardware might take additional time to reprogram.
sections.plainLanguage: Convergence is the moment one router finishes thinking and acting on the network change, not the moment packets actually start using the new route.

sections.title: Types of Network Events
sections.content:
Four types of topology changes trigger OSPF convergence. Link or neighbor up: A new link or router becomes available. The router must form adjacencies, sync the link-state database, and calculate new routes. Initialization: The OSPF process starts on a router, similar to link-up but on all links at once.

Link down: A link fails and layer 2 (the link itself) detects it immediately. Convergence is quick because failure is detected instantly. Adjacency down: The neighbor is still reachable on layer 2, but layer 3 (routing protocol) detects the failure via hello timeout. This convergence is slower because the router must wait for the dead interval to expire before confirming the neighbor is gone.
sections.plainLanguage: Links come up or go down, and routers either learn it right away or have to wait and notice the neighbor stopped saying hello.
